final:
Somewhere on Spotify, Amazon Music, Apple Music, and YouTube Music, songs were racking up billions of streams that no human ever chose to play. The royalty system paid out anyway, treating each play as if a real listener had pressed play on purpose. For years, that gap between what the platforms assumed was happening and what was actually happening quietly generated millions of dollars for one man in North Carolina.

On October 20, 2017, Michael Smith sent himself an email. Not to a partner, not to a lawyer — to himself. And what it contained was less a message than a ledger: a cold, column-by-column projection of exactly how much money his operation was going to make.

The math started small and built fast. Smith documented that he was running 52 cloud service accounts. Each one hosted 20 bot accounts, giving him 1,040 bots in total. Each bot could stream approximately 636 songs per day. Multiply those two figures together and you get 661,440 streams flowing every single day — not from listeners, not from fans stumbling onto a playlist, but from a system Smith had built to run without any of that.

From there, the royalty math was almost mundane in its precision. Smith pegged the average payout per stream at half a cent — $0.005. Carry that across a month: $99,216.

What makes the email striking is not the ambition — it's the timing. This was 2017. Smith was already running the bot infrastructure and projecting its economics, the AI catalog would come later, but the machinery to exploit it was already in place. The cloud infrastructure, the per-stream economics — he had reduced the entire operation to a formula before the formula had a name.

Before the bots, before the AI catalog, before the October 2017 email that reduced the whole operation to arithmetic, there was a musician. Smith had his own songs, his own catalog, and was based near Cornelius, North Carolina.

The paper trail shows the choice arriving early. In a May 11, 2017 email, he asked a co-conspirator to create bot accounts on a streaming platform: "Make up names and addresses[.] [J]ust make sure they all are the same for family member and also make sure everyone is over 18."

What followed ran in three documented stages: build the bot accounts, deploy software to keep them streaming continuously, then collect the royalties those fake plays generated. The AI came later. The corruption of the royalty system came first.

The foundation was identity — thousands of them, purchased in bulk from vendors who sold fake email accounts the way a wholesaler moves inventory. Each name became a bot account on a streaming platform. At certain points, Smith had as many as 10,000 active bot accounts on the streaming platforms. He paid individuals abroad and co-conspirators inside the United States to do the data-entry work of signing them up, turning registration into an outsourced assembly line.

Payment was the next problem. Smith solved that by approaching a Manhattan-based financial service that issued corporate debit cards in bulk — the kind a company distributes to employees. He lied to them. He submitted dozens of the fake names from his bot account roster and claimed they were employees of his company. The cards came back. The subscriptions went live.

He ran those subscriptions on family plans, which cost less per user than individual accounts, stretching each dollar of overhead across more active bot slots. Then he loaded the bots onto cloud computers — virtual machines he could run in parallel — with multiple browser tabs open at once, each tab logged into a separate bot account, each account streaming. To keep that streaming continuous and automatic, he purchased macros, small pieces of code that loop a task without human input, and modified them for his specific setup. The modified macros played the music on their own, indefinitely.

The last layer was concealment. Thousands of streams appeared to originate from thousands of different locations — all of them, in fact, running out of the same house. Smith's own instruction to his co-conspirators captured the priority clearly: the bots and macros needed to be "Unde[te]ctable: At least put every safety measure in to avoid detection." Smith caused the bot accounts to log in using different virtual private networks to conceal that they were all operating from his home. On October 4, 2018, he spelled out the strategy to two co-conspirators: "in order to not raise any issues with the powers that be we need a TON of content with small amounts of Streams."

By May 2019, Smith was stating the problem plainly in his own words: "I can't run the bots without content. And I need enough content so I don't overrun each song. That's the problem. If we get too many streams on one song it comes down." The machine he had built could generate hundreds of thousands of streams a day, but it had a structural weakness he couldn't engineer away: it needed songs. Not one song, but a constantly replenishing supply of distinct tracks large enough that no single title ever accumulated a suspicious play count.

Around 2018, Smith began working with two new figures: the CEO of an AI music company, identified in the indictment as CC-3, and a music promoter identified as CC-4. The approach was cautious at first. Smith began streaming AI-generated music in or about October 2018, in what CC-4 called a "proof of concept." By October 18, 2018, Smith reported hundreds of thousands of streams generated from that test, and CC-4 replied, "we've proved the model works."

What followed was industrialization. On or about February 1, 2019, Smith and CC-3 formalized the arrangement in a Master Services Agreement. Smith would own the intellectual property outright. He would supply the metadata — song titles, artist names — and pay CC-3's company either $2,000 per month or 15 percent of the streaming revenue generated from those tracks, whichever was greater. CC-3 had a financial stake in the volume Smith could push through the bots.

The songs themselves arrived as raw files — names like "n_7a2b2d74-1621-4385-895d-b1e4af78d860.mp3," randomized strings of letters and numbers that meant nothing to a listener, because no listener was ever the point. Smith's job was to dress them. Procedurally generated word combinations: "Zygophyceae," "Zygosporic," "Zyme Bedewing," "Zymotechny." Artists named "Calm Knuckles," "Calorie Screams," "Camel Edible," "Cambists Cagelings." The names had no logic, no identity, no human origin — which was precisely the point. They weren't meant to be found. They were meant to exist, to occupy a slot in a catalog, to be streamed by a bot and forgotten.

In a March 11, 2019 email, CC-3 wrote to Smith: "Keep in mind what we're doing musically here... this is not music, it's instant music;)." The winked semicolon didn't soften what he was describing.

The first warning arrived on March 6, 2018. Distribution Company-1 contacted Smith to tell him that one of his songs "fit the criteria that is usually linked to store end streaming abuse." The language was careful, almost diplomatic — criteria, usually linked — but the implication was plain. Something in his numbers had tripped a flag.

Smith wrote back the same day. "I acknowledge what you wrote and I ask that you still release it. We have no intentions of committing streaming fraud." He didn't ask which song, or which store, or what the pattern looked like. He acknowledged and denied in the same breath, as if the goal were to close the conversation before it deepened.

It didn't close. By October 2018, Distribution Company-1 came back with a harder message: it had received "multiple reports of streaming abuse from different stores" and was planning to pull his releases entirely. This time Smith dropped the measured tone. "This is absolutely wrong and crazy!... There is absolutely no fraud going on whatsoever! How can I appeal this?"

When Streaming Platform-1 made its own determination of fraud in March 2019 and informed Distribution Company-3, Smith escalated to direct confrontation. He wrote to the platform demanding proof, accusing it of slander, and insisting it had withheld money owed to him. "I have never done anything to artificially inflate my streams," he wrote — a sentence composed while thousands of bots were streaming his catalog on a loop.

By June 5, 2019, Smith was celebrating. He messaged CC-3 and CC-4: "We are at 88 million TOTAL STREAMS so far!!!" Three exclamation points. Same day, he asked CC-3 for another 10,000 AI songs so he could "spread this out more" — not a creative request, a dispersal strategy, the same logic from the October 2018 playbook applied at a larger scale.

In an August 17, 2020 email, CC-3 told Smith the song quality was "10x-20x better now," with "vocal generation capabilities."

The money moved on a loop. From approximately 2020 through 2023, Smith transferred $1.3 million in royalties into a bank account he controlled under the name SMH Entertainment, then routed those funds back out to fund debit cards for the bot accounts. Fraud financing fraud — the scheme recycling its own output to stay alive.

By February 2024, Smith wasn't managing risk anymore. He was keeping score. In an email that year, he wrote that his music had generated "over 4 billion streams and $12 million in royalties since 2019." He was bragging. He also tried to sell the scheme as a service, in which other musicians would pay him or share royalties in exchange for fraudulent streams of their music.

The indictment was unsealed on September 4, 2024. The Southern District of New York and the FBI announced three counts: wire fraud conspiracy, wire fraud, and money laundering conspiracy. For the first time, the full shape of what Smith had built was public, not a distribution company's internal flag, but a federal criminal case.

Smith later pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud. The maximum exposure under that plea: five years in prison. And then the number that gives the whole scheme its final measurement — he agreed to forfeit $8,091,843.64. Not a round figure. Not an estimate. The government said that figure represented proceeds traceable to the offense; the indictment had alleged he obtained more than $10 million in royalty payments.

U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton described the plea as covering a scheme to defraud both the streaming platforms and the musicians whose royalties Smith's fake plays had displaced. Federal regulations at 37 C.F.R. §§ 385.2 and 385.21 are explicit: manipulated streams are not eligible for royalties. Every fraudulent play Smith's bots generated was counted toward royalty payments drawn from the same pools that paid legitimate artists. The streams were fake.

Distribution Company-1 put it plainly in its own definition of streaming manipulation: plays that "do not represent bona fide end-user listening." That phrase — bona fide end-user listening — is the standard the whole system is built on. Streaming Platform-1's user guidelines prohibited any bot, script, or automated process used to artificially increase play counts. Smith's operation violated both the contractual terms and the federal regulatory framework, simultaneously, at scale, for years.

Reporting has described this prosecution as the first major criminal conviction for AI-assisted music streaming fraud in the United States. No other defendant was charged in the SDNY criminal case.

It started with an email Smith sent himself on October 20, 2017, turning bot streams into dollars. The streams were never heard. The money was real. Nearly seven years after that email, a federal indictment turned the same arithmetic into the case against him.
